events.title: East India Company founds a trading post
hints: A sparsely populated island was chosen as a free port in 1819.
Stamford Raffles signed a treaty with a local ruler and a rival claimant.
A treaty in 1824 ceded the whole island to the Company.
events.summary: In 1819 Sir Stamford Raffles of the East India Company signed a treaty establishing a trading post on the island, backed by Sultan Hussein and the Temenggong. The 1824 treaty ceded it fully to the Company, which developed it as a free port at the southern end of the Strait of Malacca.
events.quip: Rarely has so much been acquired for so few signatures and so little scrutiny.

events.title: Straits Settlements
hints: Three ports on a strait were united as one colony in 1826.
Its customs revenue depended partly on licensed opium farms.
It became a Crown colony in 1867 and was dissolved after the Second World War.
events.summary: The Straits Settlements united Penang, Malacca and Singapore from 1826 and became a Crown colony in 1867. The colony was a hub for exporting tin and rubber and for the entrepot trade, with a large share of public revenue in the early decades coming from licensed opium farms.

events.title: Syonan-to and the Sook Ching
hints: The 'impregnable fortress' fell after a week-long battle in February 1942.
The island was renamed 'Light of the South' by its new rulers.
A purge of ethnic Chinese men, the Sook Ching, killed thousands in the opening weeks.
events.summary: After the British surrender in February 1942 Japan occupied the island and renamed it Syonan-to. In the Sook Ching purge, thousands of ethnic Chinese men were killed, and the three-and-a-half-year occupation brought food shortages and repression.
